title: How to Tell If a Porcelain Sign Is Real (5-Minute Check)
description: Real porcelain signs are glass fused to iron or steel, one color at a time. Here's a 5-minute in-booth check for chips, rust, grommets and modern fakes.

hero.h1: How to spot a real vintage sign in five minutes, right in the booth
hero.lede: Old gas, road and railroad signs get reproduced — a lot. Here's how to tell an old sign from a new one dressed up to look old — with a magnet, a loupe and five minutes.

photo.alt: A vendor booth wall hung with signs, including California 32, Gall St., Phillips 66, Wells Fargo & Co. Express and AAA Approved Auto Repair, with hand planes in a wooden bin, a saw blade, hubcaps and a railroad lantern
photo.caption: One vendor's wall on our last look: Phillips 66, California 32, Wells Fargo & Co. Express and AAA Approved Auto Repair signs, plus a railroad lantern, a saw blade, hubcaps and hand planes.

sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vitreous_enamel — vitreous enamel, also called porcelain enamel, is powdered glass fused to a substrate by firing, usually 750–850 °C (1,380–1,560 °F).

https://collectorsweekly.com/articles/?p=2325 — Collectors Weekly interview with Michael Bruner (Signs of Our Past): signs started as rolled iron; porcelain is powdered glass fused onto the iron; a base coat is fired, then colors layered one on top of another; porcelain reached the U.S. in the 1890s; cost ended porcelain sign making; WWII scrap drives; 1-to-10 grading; crazing loses gloss.
https://www.collectorsweekly.com/signs/porcelain — glass layers fused color by color onto heavy rolled iron; porcelain signs dominated outdoor advertising from the 1880s until the 1950s.

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enamel_sign — enamel signs died down around WWII (cost, wartime metal); specialty makers exist today but not mass-market; value increasingly tied to condition; common damage includes scratches, bullet holes and crazing.

https://www.earlycoke.com/made-in-mumbai — Blaine Martin (Martin Guide to Vintage Coca-Cola Memorabilia): fakes from India and in some cases China or Australia; fantasy signs with no original; solid blue or solid green Coca-Cola signs never existed; overlapping enamel is called shelving and newer signs often lack it; authentic chips expose layers and dark rust, fakes show new orange rust and continuous edge chipping; grommets should not look new unless unused; compare hole positions to originals; crude or out-of-proportion logos, crude lettering and computer fonts; authentic signs usually carry a discreet maker's stamp but some newer signs add a maker's name; modern production leaves rail/tracking marks on the back and some post-1950 authentic signs have them too.

https://antiqueadvertisingexpert.com/spotting-a-fake-signclues-from-the-expert/ — Randy Huetsch: fakes get intentional chips mainly on the edges, originals chip throughout; authentic chips show layered enamel; fake rust orange-red, original black-brown; rivets that look recently made; a door push with no holes is generally fake; red fades first, so shiny red deserves caution; a magnet sticks to original steel signs and signs from the 1950s and before never used aluminum; fakes can seep a powdery residue; companies in India and the Philippines produce porcelain signs; beware vague 'vintage'/'authentic' listing language.

https://antiqueadvertisingexpert.com/project/henry-luebbe-self-framed-tin-soda-signs-1900/ — tin signs were lithographed, one color per press run; self-framed signs printed image and simulated frame on one sheet, then bent to shape.

https://www.collectorsweekly.com/stories/35096-fake-porcelain-coca-cola-signs — collector forum: a sign its owner called heavy and porcelain was confirmed fake; fakes made in sizes that differ from the original's dimensions. (Forum; used only for 'weight didn't help' and the size check.)
https://kovels.com/tag/fake-antiques — Kovels 'April Tip: Don't be Fooled by Fakes': black, red, green and blue porcelain Coca-Cola signs made in India are easy-to-spot fakes.

https://www.kovels.com/blog/words-of-wisdom-letter-to-lee/finding-fakes.html — Kovels 'Finding Fakes' (Dec 1, 2004, free excerpt): reproductions are offered in gift catalogs labeled as new, then creep into garage sales and flea markets.

https://auctions.morphyauctions.com/DRINK_COCA_COLA_FOUNTAIN_SERVICE_PORCELAIN_SIGN_-LOT595028.aspx — Morphy lot language: DSP; maker marked 'Tenn. Enamel Mfg. Corp. 1933'; shelving; touch up; per-side scores; grade categories (centering, color, edges, field, gloss, mounting holes, surface); exact dimensions listed.
https://auctions.morphyauctions.com/INDEPENDENT_OIL_PORCELAIN_TRIANGLE_SIGN_W__EAGLE_G-LOT599239.aspx — AGS-certified lot noting a non-factory mounting hole and edge porcelain loss on a genuine sign.

https://morphyauctions.com/morphys-rolls-out-premium-grade-advertising-signs-gas-pumps-and-globes-for-april-3-automobilia-petroliana-auction/ — sign marked 'Tennessee Enamel, 1931'; grades such as 9.5 out of 10 and 8.75+.
https://www.earlycoke.com/porcelain-signs-condition-guide — 1-to-10 / Mint-to-Poor condition scale definitions.

https://www.antiquetrader.com/antiques-news/antique-advertising-grading-service — AGS (Authentication & Grading Services) authenticates and grades antique advertising, including automobilia and petroliana, on a 1-to-100 scale built from a number for every aspect of an item (Sep 13, 2023).
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Provenance — provenance is the chronology of ownership, custody or location; documented provenance can help show an object has not been altered and is not a forgery.
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phillips_66 — the Phillips 66 name dates to 1927; the shield logo was introduced in 1930.

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Fargo_(1852%E2%80%931998) — the government forced Wells Fargo to consolidate its domestic express operations into American Railway Express, which began July 1, 1918.
https://www.aaa.com/aaa/222/home/faq.htm — AAA Approved Auto Repair was established in 1975.
